latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Molecular block that traps myeloid precursors at the abnormal promyelocyte stage. This is the core APL geometry, distinct from generic AML, and creates a disease state that is uniquely sensitive to differentiating therapy.

Aggregate marrow and circulating burden of abnormal promyelocytes. Drives marrow replacement, peripheral blasts/promyelocytes, leukocytosis or leukopenia patterns, leukostasis risk, and treatment-related differentiation cell flux.

Suppression of normal hematopoiesis by promyelocyte marrow expansion. Produces thrombocytopenia, anemia, neutropenia, fatigue, infection susceptibility, and fever from neutropenic or inflammatory contexts.

Promyelocyte procoagulant, annexin II-mediated fibrinolysis, tissue-factor activity, cytokine/endothelial activation, and thrombocytopenia combine to produce DIC-like bleeding risk with low fibrinogen, high D-dimer, prolonged PT/aPTT, and catastrophic hemorrhage.
Endothelial activation, platelet activation, leukemic-cell adhesion, microparticles, and DIC biology create venous and arterial thrombosis risk despite the bleeding phenotype.

High circulating promyelocyte count and cell adhesion can obstruct pulmonary, CNS, renal, or coronary microcirculation. APL leukostasis is less common than generic AML leukostasis but becomes critical with high or rapidly rising WBC.

ATRA or arsenic can rapidly drive promyelocytes into maturing myeloid cells that adhere, migrate, release cytokines, and infiltrate lung, kidney, serosa, and myocardium. This is the mechanism behind differentiation syndrome.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Early complication load from delayed APL-directed therapy and support
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Hours to days without differentiating therapy and aggressive correction of coagulopathy allow hemorrhage, thrombosis, infection, leukostasis, and organ injury to accumulate. This is the main early-death geometry of APL.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: The APL differentiation block expands abnormal promyelocytes in marrow and blood.
APL marrow is dominated by abnormal promyelocytes at diagnosis.
Peripheral smear often shows blasts or promyelocytes with cytopenias or coagulopathy.
Circulating abnormal promyelocytes may be quantified as a percentage of leukocytes.
APL can present with leukopenia, normal WBC, or marked leukocytosis; high burden and differentiating therapy can rapidly raise WBC.
Marrow packed with abnormal promyelocytes suppresses normal erythroid, megakaryocytic, and neutrophil production.
Anemia reflects marrow replacement plus bleeding.
Severe thrombocytopenia is a core APL presentation and magnifies bleeding risk.
Normal neutrophil output falls with marrow failure, increasing infection risk.
Anemia and systemic illness produce fatigue and dizziness.
Neutropenia, mucosal bleeding, and intensive therapy increase bacterial/fungal infection risk.
APL coagulopathy consumes fibrinogen and accelerates fibrinolysis.
Fibrin formation and fibrinolysis drive very high D-dimer values.
Consumptive coagulopathy prolongs PT/INR.
Severe DIC can prolong aPTT as clotting factors are consumed.
Low platelets, low fibrinogen, and fibrinolysis produce bruising, petechiae, mucosal bleeding, hematuria, GI bleeding, or ICH.
Major bleeding is the dominant early fatal complication before coagulopathy is corrected.
APL-related DIC and thrombocytopenia can cause sudden fatal intracranial hemorrhage.
Severe APL coagulopathy can manifest as GI or genitourinary bleeding.
Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage is an early catastrophic bleeding event in APL.
APL can produce venous or arterial thrombosis despite bleeding-prone DIC.
Large-artery limb or coronary thrombosis is rare but characteristic enough to model as an APL event path.
APL increases catheter-related, DVT/PE, and unusual-site thrombosis risk.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: especially when WBC is above 10-50 x10^9/L or rising rapidly during induction
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: High or rapidly increasing WBC raises leukostasis and early complication risk.
Leukostasis event risk rises with hyperleukocytosis and adhesion biology.
Pulmonary leukostasis and DS physiology reduce gas exchange.
CNS leukostasis or hemorrhage can produce focal deficits, seizure, or altered mental status.
Differentiating myeloid cells drive fever, pulmonary infiltrates, edema, hypotension, renal injury, effusions, and shock.
Differentiation syndrome often presents with fever and sepsis mimic.
Pulmonary infiltrates or edema are common severe DS manifestations.
Pulmonary capillary leak and infiltrates cause dyspnea and hypoxemic respiratory failure.
DS capillary leak, shock, inflammation, and tumor lysis can produce AKI.
Severe DS can cause shock physiology.
DS often has edema, weight gain, effusions, and volume-overload-like imaging.
Delayed APL-directed therapy and transfusion support allow coagulopathy to progress.
Early mortality in APL is dominated by delay-sensitive hemorrhage, thrombosis, infection, leukostasis, and DS.

axes.shape_free_text: Healthy 0; APL marrow often has dominant abnormal promyelocytes, commonly 30-90% of nucleated marrow cells before therapy.
Peripheral smear may show blasts or abnormal promyelocytes; morphology is not a cytogenetic/flow-confirmatory axis.
Fraction of peripheral leukocytes described as blasts or promyelocytes when quantified; not flow cytometry.
APL may present leukopenic, normal, or leukocytotic; WBC >10 x10^9/L marks higher early complication and DS risk; values can exceed 100 in hyperleukocytic APL.
High when WBC is above 10-50 x10^9/L or rising quickly during induction; drives leukostasis, DS, thrombosis, and early mortality.
Often low at presentation or during induction; recovery follows disease control and marrow recovery.
Falls from marrow failure and bleeding; severe presentations often 5-9 g/dL.
Severe thrombocytopenia is typical at diagnosis; values <30 and especially <10 x10^9/L strongly raise catastrophic bleeding risk.
Can be normal at bleeding presentation, or 38-40 degC with infection, neutropenic fever, leukemic inflammation, or differentiation syndrome.
Tachycardia rises with fever, anemia, hemorrhage, shock, DS, pulmonary edema, or sepsis mimic.
May remain normal until sudden hemorrhagic, septic, or differentiation-syndrome shock; severe DS can push MAP below 65 mmHg.
Usually normal before pulmonary complications; falls with DS pulmonary infiltrates, pulmonary hemorrhage, leukostasis, edema, or infection.
Fatigue, weakness, dizziness, or exertional intolerance from anemia, inflammation, or critical illness.
Any clinical bleeding burden: bruising, petechiae, mucosal bleeding, hematuria, vaginal bleeding, GI bleeding, pulmonary hemorrhage, or ICH.
Petechiae, purpura, or ecchymoses from thrombocytopenia and DIC.
Gingival bleeding, epistaxis, shaving/flossing bleeding, or oral mucosal bleeding.
Gross or microscopic hematuria from coagulopathy or genitourinary bleeding.
Melena, hematemesis, hematochezia, or occult GI bleeding caused or worsened by APL coagulopathy.
Seizure, focal deficit, anisocoria, coma, or herniation from ICH, thrombosis, leukostasis, or metabolic shock.
Confusion, encephalopathy, coma, posturing, or loss of consciousness from ICH, shock, leukostasis, or organ failure.
Cold painful limb, pulse deficit, sensory loss, weakness, or imaging-proven acute limb ischemia from APL-associated arterial thrombosis.
Imaging or catheterization evidence of arterial thrombosis, including limb, coronary, carotid, or intracranial arterial occlusion.
DVT, PE, catheter thrombosis, cerebral venous thrombosis, or unusual-site venous thrombosis in APL context.
Healthy 200-400; active APL coagulopathy often <150 and can be <50 mg/dL in catastrophic DIC.
Very high with APL coagulopathy and fibrinolysis; values >10-20 ug/mL FEU are common in severe DIC-like presentations.
PT/INR can be normal, mildly elevated, or markedly prolonged in severe APL coagulopathy.
aPTT may rise with severe consumptive coagulopathy, though PT/fibrinogen/D-dimer are often more prominent.
May rise with leukemic burden, tissue ischemia, hemolysis, shock, tumor lysis, or DS-related organ injury.
Usually normal initially unless shock, tumor lysis, DS, leukostasis, sepsis, or baseline kidney disease develops.
Rises with shock, severe DS, sepsis mimic, tissue ischemia, or cardiac arrest.
May be normal or rise with shock, liver injury, drug toxicity, DS, or tumor lysis.
May be normal or rise with shock, liver injury, drug toxicity, DS, or tumor lysis.
Pulmonary infiltrates, edema, effusions, or congestion during differentiation syndrome, pulmonary hemorrhage, infection, or leukostasis.
Dyspnea, wheeze, hypoxemic respiratory failure, intubation, or high-flow oxygen need in DS, leukostasis, infection, edema, or pulmonary hemorrhage.
Edema, weight gain, pulmonary vascular congestion, pleural/pericardial effusions, or capillary-leak fluid retention during differentiation syndrome.
Daily hazard of clinically major bleeding, highest during the first days before coagulopathy correction.
Daily hazard of intracranial hemorrhage or hemorrhage expansion; the dominant catastrophic early APL event.
Daily hazard of diffuse alveolar or major pulmonary bleeding under severe thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy.
Daily hazard of clinically significant GI bleeding in severe APL coagulopathy.
Daily hazard of venous or arterial thrombosis, including limb ischemia, PE/DVT, stroke, catheter thrombosis, and coronary thrombosis.
Daily hazard of clinically important leukostasis, highest with high or rapidly rising WBC and organ symptoms.
Daily hazard of differentiation syndrome after ATRA/ATO exposure, peaking in the first 2 weeks and amplified by high/rising WBC or renal dysfunction.
Daily hazard of bacterial or fungal infection during neutropenia, mucosal injury, ICU care, or induction therapy; can mimic or overlap DS.
Daily hazard of AKI from DS, shock, tumor lysis, sepsis, leukostasis, nephrotoxins, or baseline renal vulnerability.

Lifespan outcome hazard for APL. Peaks in the first days to 2 weeks from hemorrhage, thrombosis, leukostasis, infection, organ failure, or differentiation syndrome; falls sharply after coagulopathy control and effective APL-directed therapy.
Elapsed time from bleeding/infectious/fatigue symptom onset or abnormal CBC recognition to APL-directed therapy and coagulopathy support.
Clinical suspicion from smear morphology, Auer rods, promyelocytes, cytopenias, and coagulopathy. This is not PML-RARA, flow, or cytogenetic confirmation.
Current major bleeding or high-risk bleeding anatomy, including ICH, pulmonary hemorrhage, GI bleeding, or uncontrolled genitourinary bleeding.
High-risk APL treatment context from WBC >10 x10^9/L or rapidly rising WBC during induction.
Risk context for arsenic-related QT toxicity: baseline QT prolongation, interacting drugs, hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia, or unstable arrhythmia.
Ability to safely deliver arsenic trioxide in the presence of hepatic injury, renal impairment, electrolyte instability, and ICU organ failure.
Ability to safely deliver anthracycline cytoreduction in the presence of cardiomyopathy, active MI, arrhythmia, severe shock, or frailty.
Ability to deliver hydroxyurea, anthracycline, or other cytoreductive therapy when WBC is high or rising.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Lower platelets directly increase mucosal, surgical, pulmonary, GI, and intracranial bleeding hazard.
Low fibrinogen is central to APL catastrophic bleeding risk.
Fibrinolysis produces simultaneous high D-dimer and low fibrinogen.
When global major bleeding hazard is high, ICH and ICH expansion are more likely.
Major bleeding is a dominant early cause of death in APL.
ICH is a highly fatal early complication and can dominate lifespan outcome.
High or rising WBC during induction predicts differentiation syndrome.
Severe DS commonly manifests as pulmonary edema, infiltrates, or effusions.
DS capillary leak and shock raise AKI hazard.
Severe DS can produce respiratory failure, shock, AKI, and cardiac arrest.
High or rapidly rising WBC increases leukostasis hazard.
Pulmonary/CNS leukostasis can be rapidly fatal.
Coronary, pulmonary, CNS, or limb thrombosis can cause early death or irreversible organ injury.
Fever, anemia, DS, and infection contexts commonly move temperature and heart rate together.
Infection and sepsis mimic are major competing hazards during APL cytopenia and induction.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: ATRA benefit begins before molecular confirmation when morphology plus coagulopathy strongly suggests APL.
Delay-sensitive coagulopathy means earlier ATRA changes early bleeding hazard.
Severe DS may require temporary ATRA interruption while steroids and organ support control the inflammatory vector.

side_effects.interpretation: Differentiating promyelocytes can trigger DS, especially with high/rising WBC.
ATRA exposure raises DS hazard while lowering coagulopathy and long-term disease hazard.

treatments.context_specific_role: Directly reshapes the APL differentiation-arrest landscape and rapidly improves coagulopathy when started early.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Arsenic can prolong QT; electrolyte correction and ECG monitoring modulate safe delivery.
Severe renal/hepatic dysfunction or ICU instability may require interruption or careful modification.
ATO can also contribute to DS biology.

side_effects.interpretation: Arsenic increases QT and arrhythmia risk in susceptible contexts.
ATO can precipitate or amplify DS.

treatments.context_specific_role: Disease-reshaping differentiating/apoptotic therapy, especially important in non-high-risk or ATRA/ATO strategies.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Cytoreduction directly lowers WBC-driven DS/leukostasis/thrombosis pressure.
Active MI, cardiomyopathy, or shock may make anthracycline unsafe.

side_effects.interpretation: Cytotoxic therapy deepens cytopenias before marrow recovery.
Neutropenia and mucosal injury increase infectious hazard.

treatments.context_specific_role: Rapidly reduces promyelocyte and WBC burden when high/rising WBC is driving DS, leukostasis, or thrombosis pressure.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Hydroxyurea directly targets high or rapidly rising WBC while definitive induction is assembled.
Severe organ failure or inability to take oral medication reduces feasibility.

treatments.context_specific_role: Short-interval WBC pressure relief when high/rising WBC amplifies leukostasis or differentiation-syndrome hazards.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Active bleeding shifts support toward aggressive platelet, cryoprecipitate/fibrinogen, and plasma replacement.
Large transfusion volumes can worsen pulmonary edema or DS-like fluid overload.

side_effects.interpretation: Large-volume plasma/cryoprecipitate support can worsen edema or pulmonary congestion.
Correction of bleeding risk must be balanced against APL thrombotic biology.

treatments.context_specific_role: Pushes hemostatic state immediately while ATRA/ATO reshape the disease geometry.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Steroids directly counter the inflammatory DS vector.
Steroids can worsen occult infection, so antimicrobial coverage and source evaluation modify net outcome.

side_effects.interpretation: High-dose steroids can worsen bacterial or fungal infection risk.
Steroid demargination can transiently raise measured WBC.

treatments.context_specific_role: Directly suppresses the DS inflammatory vector and protects organ axes while APL therapy is adjusted.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Empiric antimicrobial coverage and culture-directed treatment lower infection-driven mortality.
Oxygen, ventilation, diuresis, or ICU monitoring directly stabilize respiratory failure while causal treatment works.

treatments.context_specific_role: Stabilizes infection, respiratory, renal, shock, and ICU axes that decide early RMST while APL-specific therapy reshapes disease mechanisms.

present.trajectory_modulation: High or rapidly rising WBC is a high-risk APL context for DS, leukostasis, thrombosis, and early death.
Delay in ATRA and coagulopathy support allows early hemorrhagic and thrombotic hazards to accumulate.
Older or frail patients have less reserve for bleeding, infection, DS, and cardiopulmonary complications.
Atherosclerosis or stents provide substrate for APL-associated arterial thrombosis.
Renal dysfunction predicts severe DS and reduces tolerance for arsenic, fluids, tumor lysis, and shock.
Infection can mimic DS and add a second early hazard during APL cytopenia and induction.
Obesity or limited cardiopulmonary reserve can amplify respiratory consequences of DS and transfusion/volume support.

supportive_care: Treat APL coagulopathy as a continuous early hazard: frequent CBC, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer, renal, liver, and cardiopulmonary monitoring during induction.
Use platelet, cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen replacement, and plasma support to keep hemostatic axes out of catastrophic ranges while ATRA/ATO reduce the coagulopathy vector.
Monitor for DS daily during ATRA/ATO exposure, especially high/rising WBC, fever, dyspnea, pulmonary infiltrates, edema, hypotension, renal injury, effusions, or sudden shock.
Use cytoreduction when WBC is high or rising; the causal target is promyelocyte/WBC burden, DS hazard, leukostasis hazard, and thrombotic pressure.
Evaluate fever and pulmonary findings as both DS and infection until evidence separates them; antimicrobial and ICU support modify secondary infection and shock hazards.
Avoid invasive procedures when possible until platelets, fibrinogen, and coagulopathy are corrected; when unavoidable, model the added bleeding hazard through event axes.
